decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has six short lessons. First, checking a paraphrase against its original source. Second, judging whether a reference list's range reflects real research scope. Third, paraphrasing a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. Fourth, working out what an unfamiliar source type needs. Fifth, referencing an unfamiliar source correctly under time pressure. Sixth, gathering and citing sources that support and challenge a position. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the six lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
By now you should be comfortable with the basics of referencing: naming sources, matching a style, and spotting an inconsistent citation. This course builds on that. It moves from getting referencing right to judging it: checking a paraphrase properly against its original, weighing whether a reference list's range reflects the real scope of someone's research, and working out how to reference a source that does not fit a standard template.

By the end you will be able to check a paraphrase against its source, judge whether a reference list's range reflects real research scope, paraphrase a technical passage for a non-specialist reader, work out what an unfamiliar source needs, reference it correctly under time pressure, and gather and cite sources that both support and challenge a position.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Six flat learning outcomes, read from crs-07_tiered-outcomes (pathway-distillation profile: crs-03 is not-applicable), framed up front: checking a paraphrase against its source, judging reference-list range, paraphrasing a technical passage for a non-specialist, handling an unfamiliar source type, referencing under time pressure, and citing both sides of a position.

practiceConnection.academic: Checking a paraphrase, judging a reference list's range, and working out how to cite something unfamiliar are not one-off exam skills: you will meet them across every module that asks for independent reading, from literature reviews to group projects with mixed source types. The judgement you build here also feeds directly into how you handle sources when researching and when writing critically, where the same questions about range, attribution and traceability come up again.

decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Referencing is no longer just about getting the mechanics right: you can now check a paraphrase against its source, judge whether a reference list's range reflects the real scope of someone's research, paraphrase a technical passage for a non-specialist reader, work out what an unfamiliar source needs, reference it correctly under time pressure, and gather sources that support and challenge a position. That judgement builds directly on the accuracy and consistency you brought from the introductory course. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: Apply this judgement the next time you draft a literature review or a group report with mixed source types: check your own paraphrases against their originals, weigh whether your reading list's range reflects the scope of the question, and work out an unfamiliar source's citation from first principles rather than forcing it into a template. The same judgement about range and traceability is exactly what you draw on when finding and using sources for a longer project, and when researching a topic that calls for a documented method.

decidedValue.whereNextBody: This course has assumed the introductory groundwork: naming sources accurately, matching a style, and spotting an inconsistent citation. If any of that still feels shaky, the introductory course is there to revisit. Moving on, the advanced course in this pathway turns from getting the judgement right to acting on it under pressure: the ethical choices that referencing and attribution raise once you are working independently, in shared work, or in a professional role.

items.stem: A student rewrites a source sentence by swapping a few words but keeping its structure and most phrasing. What should checking the paraphrase against its original reveal?
A reference list cites several sources that all support the same conclusion, with no opposing view represented. What does evaluating its range suggest?
You are paraphrasing a technical passage for a reader unfamiliar with the field. What must the paraphrase still do?
You need to reference an unfamiliar source type with no obvious template. What should you identify first?
You must reference an unfamiliar source type under time pressure. What should you do, beyond getting an answer quickly?
A recommendation is backed only by sources that agree with it. What does gathering and citing opposing sources as well let a reader do?
